units.text: You’ll learn how Lambda starts, how long it can run, and which identity controls access. Synchronous callers wait. Direct asynchronous calls queue an event. An event source mapping polls the source and invokes the function with records.

Now compare the runtime rows. An on-demand Event Function can run for up to thirty minutes per invocation. Managed Instances use Lambda-managed E C two capacity in your account: up to thirty minutes synchronously, or ninety for direct asynchronous invocation and supported event source mappings. Amazon MQ and DocumentDB mappings are exceptions at fifteen minutes.

Durable Functions checkpoint steps and can suspend and resume; a direct asynchronous durable execution can span up to a year, not one year of continuous compute. A Web Function has a separate fifteen-minute limit per HTTP request. Check your A P I or caller timeout independently.

Follow the two locks. If EventBridge cannot start the function, check permission to invoke the intended function or alias and scope the grant to the expected source. If the function starts but cannot read the secret, check its execution role and the secret’s policy instead. The caller’s invocation grant cannot authorize what the handler does. Keep secret values out of logs.

You’ll learn to choose an A P I type and connect requests to a backend without giving clients direct access to that backend. Follow the client into A P I Gateway. The gateway matches a route or method, applies the configured authorization and throttling, then calls Lambda or another supported backend.

For example, the same front door can accept the client’s order request without giving that client permission to invoke a function directly. Separate the gateway’s decision to admit the caller from its permission to reach the backend.

Choose from the requirement, not the name. This REST column fits an A P I that needs usage plans, request validation, stage caching, direct WAF association, or a private REST endpoint. HTTP APIs can serve a simpler request-response interface, including JWT authorization when supported.

Do not assume an HTTP A P I includes the REST feature set. A WebSocket A P I holds a persistent connection for two-way messages. For a live chat, the backend may need to send an update without waiting for another HTTP request. That makes the connection lifecycle and callback permissions part of the design.

The integration is a separate contract from the client-facing route. Trace the three backend choices. A Lambda proxy can pass a request event to code. A direct A W S service operation maps the request to a specific action. An HTTP integration calls a compatible HTTP endpoint and must be able to reach it.

Decide where request mapping, validation, and error translation occur. Importing an OpenAPI document can define the shape of the A P I, but it does not give A P I Gateway permission to invoke a backend or make a private endpoint reachable.

In the queue intake example, the upper comparison uses a function only to forward the payload. A supported direct integration can map that request into S Q S SendMessage using an integration role limited to the intended queue.

The caller receives an acceptance response, not proof that a worker processed the message. Test both a valid request and a rejected request before removing the function. Keep Lambda when custom validation, orchestration, or business transformations cannot be expressed by the direct integration contract.

You’ll learn to release A P I and function changes independently, then choose a transfer path that fits the payload. Trace the A P I stage to its deployment, then trace the qualified integration target to a Lambda alias. The stage chooses the published A P I configuration.

The alias can distribute function invocations across versions. A P I canary settings and alias weights are independent: rolling back one does not automatically undo the other. Check the stage, deployed route, alias, and invocation permissions when a release takes unexpected traffic.

Follow the request through all three gates. A standard buffered REST A P I has a ten-megabyte payload ceiling. A buffered synchronous Lambda invocation has a separate six-megabyte request and response ceiling; the event and response encoding take space too. The usual REST integration timeout is twenty-nine seconds, but Regional and private REST integrations can request an increase, which may require reducing the account-level throttle quota.

A supported REST proxy can stream the response for up to fifteen minutes and beyond the usual buffered response ceiling. Idle timeouts still apply, and request streaming is not supported. Check A P I type, integration, and caller rather than quoting one universal limit.

In the upload flow, authorize the client first, then sign a short-lived request for the intended object key, method, and required headers. The browser sends the object body straight to S three; A P I Gateway and Lambda are out of that data path.

Treat the URL like a bearer credential, because whoever holds it can try the scoped operation while it remains valid. Verify the stored key, size, and checksum as required before accepting the upload downstream. A successful response from the signing A P I proves only that the capability was issued.

Separate how the client reaches A P I Gateway from how the gateway reaches the backend. Edge-optimized REST uses managed edge locations to reach one regional A P I. A Regional A P I can sit behind your own CloudFront distribution. A private REST A P I uses a reachable execute-api interface endpoint. Choose by the client's location and trust boundary. An edge-optimized endpoint is not a design for separate backends in multiple Regions.

For private REST, verify D N S, routing and the interface endpoint security group. The endpoint policy limits passage; the A P I resource policy and method authorization are separate gates. The A P I can require the expected endpoint and still require an authorized caller. If it connects but is denied, inspect those policies rather than replacing the route.
A public REST A P I can reach a private backend through a version two V P C link. A private REST endpoint instead controls client ingress and does not configure that integration.

Check same-account ownership, listener compatibility, security groups and the TLS server name for H T T P S. If the backend receives the wrong path, check whether the stage prefix needs an override. Private integration and private ingress solve different problems; choosing one does not require the other.

Start with cache isolation. Two requests for the same path can need different tenant or response variants. Configure REST stage cache keys to reflect those differences, or skip caching if you cannot do so safely. Default expiry is three hundred seconds, the maximum is thirty-six hundred, and zero disables caching. Test two authorized tenants and confirm which response each receives. Use the actual method response and cache hit-and-miss evidence rather than assuming isolation from configuration alone.

An A W S caller can use an authorized I A M identity and a Signature Version Four request. A REST A P I can use a Cognito user pool or Lambda authorizer. An HTTP A P I can use a compatible JWT, I A M or Lambda authorizer.

The application still enforces access to the specific record. Test an authenticated caller requesting a record they do not own. Keep the signing credentials private; the signed request proves identity without exposing the secret key.

Three different controls protect this path. A compatible REST resource policy and method authorization determine who can invoke the A P I. The integration needs scoped permission for its backend action. D N S and a compatible ACM certificate establish the H T T P S connection, not permission. If the front door responds but Lambda is not invoked, inspect the integration grant. This can fail even if client authentication and certificate validation both succeeded.

A browser may send an OPTIONS preflight before a cross-origin request. Return the right CORS headers on preflight and actual responses; with credentials, use an explicit permitted origin rather than a wildcard. Command-line clients do not enforce CORS. Keep the real authorization check, and use server evidence to tell whether a blocked browser response was already processed. In a browser trace, distinguish a failed preflight from a successful request whose response the browser refuses to expose.

An A P I key identifies the consumer for metering, throttling and quota targets on associated REST methods and stages. It does not authorize a user or tenant. Usage-plan limits are best effort, not a hard spending cap. Test a valid key with invalid authorization and expect rejection. Separate usage-plan targets, account limits and downstream capacity when deciding how to handle throttling.
